prompt: The section calls the activity a relative measure. What does it measure equilibrium relative to?

choices.text: A standard state
The pure solvent at its boiling point
choices.why: The boiling point plays no part in defining activity. Activity measures equilibrium relative to a standard state, which IUPAC defines.

choices.text: The total concentration of the solution
choices.why: The total concentration changes from one solution to the next. Activity is measured against a fixed reference, the standard state.

choices.text: An ideal gas at 0 °C and 1 atm
choices.why: Those are old reference conditions for gas volumes, not the reference for activity. Activity measures equilibrium relative to a standard state.

explanation: Activity is not an absolute quantity: it measures equilibrium relative to a standard state. That is why the standard state is defined by IUPAC and followed systematically by chemists around the globe.

prompt: According to the section, in terms of which behavior is the standard state of a solute in a solution defined?

choices.text: Its behavior at infinite dilution
Its behavior when the solution is saturated
choices.why: A saturated solution is as concentrated as it can get, and its solute particles interact strongly. The standard state is defined by infinite-dilution behavior instead.

choices.text: Its behavior in a real 1 mol/L solution
choices.why: In a real 1 mol/L solution the solute particles interact, so it is generally non-ideal. The standard state is defined by infinite-dilution behavior.

choices.text: Its behavior as an ideal gas at 1 bar
choices.why: A pressure of 1 bar is the standard state for a gas. For a solute in a solution, the standard state is defined by infinite-dilution behavior.

explanation: The standard state for a solution is defined in terms of infinite-dilution behavior. In that limit the solute particles are so far apart that they do not interact with each other.

prompt: The solute standard state is defined by infinite-dilution behavior, yet the standard concentration is 1 mol/L. How does the section reconcile the two?

choices.text: A hypothetical 1 mol/L solution behaving as if infinitely dilute
A real 1 mol/L solution, carefully prepared and measured in the lab
choices.why: A real 1 mol/L solution has solute–solute interactions, so it lacks infinite-dilution properties. The standard state is a hypothetical solution, not a real one.

choices.text: A 1 mol/L solution found by extrapolating from the pure solute
choices.why: The pure solute is not the reference here. The standard state is a hypothetical 1 mol/L solution in which the solute keeps its infinite-dilution properties.

choices.text: Whichever real concentration happens to give the solute γ = 1
choices.why: The standard state is fixed at 1 mol/L, not chosen solution by solution. It is a hypothetical 1 mol/L solution with infinite-dilution properties.

explanation: The standard state is a hypothetical solution of 1 mol/L in which the solute has infinite-dilution properties. No real 1 mol/L solution behaves this way, but the definition keeps both the familiar concentration and the ideal behavior of infinite dilution.

prompt: In the hypothetical 1 mol/L standard-state solution, the solute has infinite-dilution properties. Which property does the section give as an example?

choices.text: Solute particles do not interact with each other
Solute particles do not interact with the solvent
choices.why: Each dissolved particle is surrounded by solvent and interacts with it, even at infinite dilution. What vanishes are the interactions between solute particles.

choices.text: Solute particles pair up as they would at 1 mol/L
choices.why: Pairing up is a solute–solute interaction, which infinite dilution removes. In the standard state the solute particles do not interact with each other.

choices.text: The solute has the vapor pressure of the pure solute
choices.why: Infinite-dilution properties come from the solute particles being far apart, not from the pure solute. In the standard state they do not interact with each other.

explanation: At infinite dilution the solute particles are so far apart that they do not interact with each other. The standard state carries this property over to a concentration of 1 mol/L, which no real solution could do.

prompt: With the solute standard state defined by infinite-dilution behavior, what does an activity coefficient that is not equal to 1 describe?

choices.text: All of the solute's non-ideal behavior
Only the error in measuring the concentration
choices.why: γ is not a correction for measurement error. Since the standard state has no solute–solute interactions, γ ≠ 1 describes all of the non-ideal behavior.

choices.text: The part of the activity that is ideal
choices.why: The ideal part is already carried by the concentration. γ carries what is left: all of the non-ideal behavior.

choices.text: The change from molarity to molality units
choices.why: Changing concentration units is a separate matter. Here γ describes all of the non-ideal behavior, measured against a standard state with no solute–solute interactions.

explanation: Because the standard state already behaves ideally, with no solute–solute interactions, any departure from it shows up in the activity coefficient. So γ ≠ 1 describes all of the non-ideal behavior, and γ = 1 means the solute behaves as it would at infinite dilution.
